role: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, project sponsor and EIS preparer
stance_basis: HUD authored the EIS, prepared responses defending the project's analysis, and explicitly rebutted DOT objections to justify including the Downtown Expressway as a relevant environmental consideration
summary: HUD is the project sponsor and EIS preparer for the Randolph Urban Renewal Project, and in this chapter it responds to comments from other agencies. HUD defends its methodology, particularly its decision to analyze the Downtown Expressway's impacts on the project area, citing NEPA requirements and EPA confirmation. HUD also addresses requests for additional air quality data, traffic documentation, and noise analysis clarifications, explaining constraints while maintaining the validity of its assessments.
complaint_summary: HUD rejects DOT's assertion that the Downtown Expressway is irrelevant to the Randolph EIS, arguing that NEPA and HUD guidelines require assessment of the expressway as part of the project environment, and that EPA has confirmed this approach.

statement.text:
We must take exception to the Department of Transportation's assertion that the Downtown Expressway is not a relevant consideration in the Randolph Environmenal Impact Statement. Section 102(2)C of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 requires specifically that an 102(2)C statement on major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment assess "any adverse environmental effects which cannot be avoided should the proposal be implemented." HUD guidelines, as set forth in the document 'A Guide to Making An Environmental Evaluation and Preparing an Environmental Impact Statement" has defined "impact" explicitly: "There are three elements which can be distinguished for each impact: (a) impact of the existing environment on the viability and livability of the project; (2) impact of the project on the environment; and (3) impacts among project components." It is obvious that one of the potential negative impacts may be the wasteful allocation of federal and local money in development of housing in an unsuitable living environment. This possibility must be fully investigated in the review process, which will be used to determine whether or not the project will receive 1 HUD funding.
In this particular case the Downtown Expressway is scheduled to have completed construction before the majority of project plans are implemented in Randolph. The Expressway must therefore be considered an aspect of the environment of the project area and given an objective evaluation as such. The Environmental Protection Agency has specifically confirmed the need for analyzing the consequences of the Expressway in their letter of April 11, 1973: "As you know, assessing the environmental consequence of HUD action often requires detailed study of the impact of other projects on the environs which eventually surround HUD-assisted residents . . . HUD correctly investigated the noise and an impacts of the expressway on Randolph." The Federal Highway Administration should contact the Council on Environmental Quality for further clarification of the provisions of the National Environmental Policy Act in this regard.
